items.title: Going down a group does NOT always mean smaller ionisation energy
items.claim: First ionisation energies generally decrease down a group as the outer electron sits in a larger, more shielded orbital. Yet gold's first IE (890 kJ/mol) is HIGHER than silver's (731), and silver is higher than copper's (745) is debatable.
items.prompt: Why do the textbook trends break down here?

options.text: Relativistic contraction of the 6s orbital in heavy elements (gold, mercury) lowers the outer electron's energy, making it more tightly bound than a non-relativistic shielding picture would predict
Gold is not really in Group 11
Outer electrons of gold are pulled by nuclear charge alone

items.reveal:
Simple shielding arguments predict each row's outer electron should be easier to remove than the row above. They work moderately well for s-block and p-block. They fail for heavy transition metals and post-transition metals where relativistic effects matter.

Gold's 6s orbital contracts and becomes more 'core-like'. Its first ionisation energy rises. Mercury is similar.

Another counter-trend: across a period, IE generally rises, but boron < beryllium (because B's outer electron is in a higher-energy 2p, while Be's is in the lower 2s); oxygen < nitrogen (pairing penalty in O's half-filled 2p4 vs N's stable 2p3 half-filled).
items.why: Periodic trends are taught as smooth ladders. Real data has dips and bumps that diagnose deeper physics.

items.title: The Joliot-Curies made elements radioactive on demand in 1934
items.claim: In January 1934 Irène Joliot-Curie (daughter of Marie) and her husband Frédéric Joliot bombarded aluminium foil with alpha particles. After removing the source, the foil continued emitting radiation — they had created phosphorus-30, a radioactive isotope that does not occur in nature.

options.text: Until then, all known radioactive elements occurred naturally. The Joliot-Curies showed any element could potentially be made radioactive by nuclear bombardment, opening the field of artificial isotopes for medicine, research and weapons
It produced the first synthetic element
It was unrelated to their parents' work

items.reveal:
Alpha + aluminium-27 → phosphorus-30 + neutron. P-30 decays with a half-life of 2.5 minutes to silicon-30 by positron emission — discovered along the way.

The Joliot-Curies won the 1935 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, sharing it as a couple as Marie and Pierre had done in 1903.

Fermi (Rome, 1934) extended the work using neutrons as projectiles, producing many new isotopes including (he claimed) transuranic elements. He had actually produced uranium fission products — discovered as such by Hahn, Strassmann and Meitner in 1938.

Irène died in 1956 of leukaemia, almost certainly from radiation exposure. Frédéric died in 1958 of liver disease, also linked to radiation. Two generations of Curie women died of their work.
items.why: Until 1934, radioactivity was a property of certain natural elements. After 1934, it was a tool — at the cost of the lives of those who developed it.

items.title: Wöhler made urea without a kidney in 1828
items.claim: Chemists in the 1820s believed organic compounds — substances found in living things — required a 'vital force' to be made. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler, trying to make ammonium cyanate from inorganic precursors, accidentally produced urea — an organic substance found in mammalian urine.
items.prompt: Why did Wöhler's accident matter so much?

options.text: It made an organic compound from purely inorganic starting materials — the first crack in the doctrine that living things were chemically inaccessible to laboratory synthesis

items.reveal_title: The vital force begins to crack
items.reveal:
Wöhler had been heating ammonium chloride with silver cyanate. The product crystallised as colourless prisms. Analysis showed it was identical to urea — excreted by mammalian kidneys and definitively 'organic'.

He wrote to Berzelius: 'I must tell you that I can prepare urea without requiring a kidney of an animal, either man or dog.'

The vital force doctrine didn't die overnight. Urea is a borderline case — small, simple. But later syntheses (Kolbe's acetic acid in 1845, Berthelot's full organic synthesis programme in the 1850s-60s, Miller-Urey's amino acid synthesis in 1953) extended the principle until vitalism was indefensible.

Organic chemistry became 'the chemistry of carbon compounds', not 'the chemistry of life'.
items.why: A single accidental synthesis began the demolition of a centuries-old philosophical boundary between living and non-living chemistry.
